test_text.title: A new role for livestock guard dogs

article.title: A new role for livestock guard dogs

items.sentence_raw: For thousands of years, livestock guard dogs worked alongside shepherds to protect their sheep, goats and cattle from predators such as wolves and bears.
But in the 19th and 20th centuries, when such predators were largely exterminated, most guard dogs lost their jobs.
In recent years, however, as increased efforts have been made to protect wild animals, predators have become more widespread again.
As a result, farmers once more need to protect their livestock, and guard dogs are enjoying an unexpected revival.
Today there are around 50 breeds of guard dogs on duty in various parts of the world.
These dogs are raised from an early age with the animals they will be watching and eventually these animals become the dog's family.
items.explain: Q31: The question asks for how guard dogs gain their skills. The passage says dogs are *'raised from an early age with the animals they will be watching'* and get *'initial training'* to understand livestock is their life. **'raised with livestock and initial training'** is how they gain skills. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The dogs will place themselves between the livestock and any threat, barking loudly.
items.explain: Q29: The question asks for how guard dogs' methods keep predators away. The passage says dogs *'place themselves between the livestock and any threat, barking loudly'* and *'chase away predators'* if needed. These are the methods dogs use. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: If necessary, they will chase away predators, but often their mere presence is sufficient.
items.explain: Q29: The question asks for how guard dogs' methods keep predators away. The passage says dogs *'place themselves between the livestock and any threat, barking loudly'* and *'chase away predators'* if needed. These are the methods dogs use. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "Their initial training is to make them understand that livestock is going to be their life," says Dan Macon, a shepherd with three guard dogs.
items.explain: Q31: The question asks for how guard dogs gain their skills. The passage says dogs are *'raised from an early age with the animals they will be watching'* and get *'initial training'* to understand livestock is their life. **'raised with livestock and initial training'** is how they gain skills. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "A fluffy white puppy is fun to be around, but too much human affection makes it a great dog for guarding the front porch, rather than a great livestock guard dog."
items.explain: Q36: The statement says training a livestock guard dog needs a different focus from training a house guard dog. Dan Macon says too much human affection makes a dog good for *'guarding the front porch'* (a house guard dog) instead of a livestock guard dog — this means the training focus is different. So the answer is **A (Dan Macon)**.

items.sentence_raw: The evidence indicates that guard dogs are highly effective.

For example, in Portugal, biologist Silvia Ribeiro has found that more than 90 per cent of the farmers participating in a programme to train and use guard dogs to protect their herds against attack from wolves rate the performance of the dogs as very good or excellent.
items.explain: Q30: The question asks for different academics' claims that guard dogs successfully protect herds. The passage shows two academics from separate studies: one found 90% of farmers rated dogs *'very good or excellent'*, the other found 65% of herders saw predation stop completely. These are claims that guard dogs work well. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In a study carried out in Australia by Linda van Bommel and Chris Johnson at the University of Tasmania, more than 65 per cent of herders reported that predation stopped completely after they got the dogs, and almost all the rest saw a decrease in attacks.
items.explain: Q30: The question asks for different academics' claims that guard dogs successfully protect herds. The passage shows two academics from separate studies: one found 90% of farmers rated dogs *'very good or excellent'*, the other found 65% of herders saw predation stop completely. These are claims that guard dogs work well. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: "If they are managed and used properly, livestock guard dogs are the most efficient control method that we have in terms of the amount of livestock that they save from predation," says van Bommel.
items.explain: Q35: The statement says guard dogs are the best way to protect farm animals if handled appropriately. Linda van Bommel says *'If they are managed and used properly, livestock guard dogs are the most efficient control method'* — **'managed and used properly'** means **'appropriately handled'**, **'most efficient'** means **'best way'**. So the answer is **C (Linda van Bommel)**.

items.sentence_raw: But today's guard dogs also have a new role - to help preserve the predators.
It is hoped that reductions in livestock losses can make farmers more tolerant of predators and less likely to kill them.
In Namibia, more than 90 per cent of cheetahs live outside protected areas, close to humans raising livestock.
As a result, the cheetahs are often held responsible for animal losses, and large numbers have been killed by farmers.
When guard dogs were introduced, more than 90 per cent of farmers reported a dramatic reduction in livestock losses, and said that as a result they were less likely to kill predators.
items.explain: Q27: The question asks for an example of a predator protected by guard dogs. The passage says when guard dogs were introduced, farmers were *'less likely to kill predators'* — **'less likely to kill'** means **'protected'**. The example in this part of the text refers to cheetahs in Namibia. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Julie Young, at Utah State University in the US, believes this result applies widely.
"There is common ground from the livestock perspective and from the conservation perspective," she says.
"If ranchers don't have a dead cow, they will not make a call to apply for a permit to kill a wolf."
items.explain: Q32: The statement says guard dogs may save both livestock and wild animals. Julie Young says *'If ranchers don't have a dead cow, they will not make a call to apply for a permit to kill a wolf'* — this means livestock (cows) and wild animals (wolves) are both saved. So the answer is **D (Julie Young)**.

items.sentence_raw: Looking at all the published evidence, Bethany Smith at Nottingham Trent University in the UK found that up to 88 per cent of farmers said they no longer killed predators after using dogs - but warned that such self-reported results must be taken with a pinch of salt.
items.explain: Q33: The statement says farmers' self-reported behaviour changes may not be totally accurate. Bethany Smith says self-reported results *'must be taken with a pinch of salt'* — **'taken with a pinch of salt'** means **'not totally accurate'**. So the answer is **E (Bethany Smith)**.

items.sentence_raw: What's more, it is possible that livestock guard dogs merely displace predators to unprotected neighbouring properties, where their fate isn't recorded.
"In some regions, we work with almost every farmer, but in others only one or two have dogs," says Ribeiro.
"If we are not working with everybody, we are transferring the wolf pressure to the neighbour's herd and he can use poison and kill an entire pack of wolves."
items.explain: Q34: The statement says negative results may happen if guard dog use is not widespread enough. Silvia Ribeiro says *'If we are not working with everybody, we are transferring the wolf pressure to the neighbour's herd and he can use poison and kill an entire pack of wolves'* — this describes a negative result when not all farmers use dogs. So the answer is **B (Silvia Ribeiro)**.

items.sentence_raw: Another concern is whether there may be unintended ecological effects of using guard dogs.
Studies suggest that reducing deaths of one type of predator may have a negative impact on other species.
The extent of this problem isn't known, but the consequences are clear in Namibia.
Cheetahs aren't the only species that cause sheep and goat losses there: other predators also attack livestock.
In 2015, researchers reported that in spite of the impact farmers obtaining guard dogs had on cheetahs, the number of jackals killed by dogs and people actually increased.
items.explain: Q37: The question asks which other predator's deaths rose in Namibia after guard dogs were introduced. The passage says *'the number of jackals killed by dogs and people actually increased'*. So the answer is **jackals**.

items.sentence_raw: Guard dogs have other ecological impacts too.
They have been found to spread diseases to wild animals, including endangered Ethiopian wolves.
items.explain: Q38: The question asks what dogs could spread that affects other species. The passage says *'They have been found to spread diseases to wild animals'*. So the answer is **diseases**.

items.sentence_raw: They may also compete with other carnivores for food.
items.explain: Q39: The question asks what resource dogs may reduce for wild animals. The passage says *'They may also compete with other carnivores for food'* — competing for food means less food is available for other animals. So the answer is **food**.

items.sentence_raw: And by creating a 'landscape of fear', their mere presence can influence the behaviour of prey animals.
The evidence so far, however, indicates that these consequences aren't always negative.
Guard dogs can deliver unexpected benefits by protecting vulnerable wildlife from predators.
For example, their presence has been found to protect birds which build their nests on the ground in fields, where foxes would normally raid them.
items.explain: Q40: The question asks which predator would normally raid bird nests. The passage says birds nest on the ground *'where foxes would normally raid them'*. So the answer is **foxes**.

items.sentence_raw: Indeed, Australian researchers are now using dogs to enhance biodiversity and create refuges for species threatened by predation.
So if we can get this right, there may be a bright future for guard dogs in promoting harmonious coexistence between humans and wildlife.
items.explain: Q28: The question asks for an optimistic suggestion about future positive developments for guard dogs. The passage says there may be a *'bright future'* for guard dogs to help humans and wildlife live together peacefully — **'bright future'** means **'optimistic suggestion about positive developments'**. So the answer is **G**.

subtitles: Livestock guard dogs, traditionally used to protect farm animals from predators, are now being used to protect the predators themselves
